chunks: "Both hurt the cell, in different ways. If you overcharge a LiPo, above about 4.
2 volts, you're pulling too much lithium out of the cathode, which destabilizes it, and the anode can't take more lithium so it plates as metal.
The electrolyte also starts to oxidize and produce gas, so the pouch swells. All of that makes heat, and in the worst case you get thermal runaway and fire.
So overcharge is the dangerous one. If you overdischarge, below roughly 3. 0 volts and certainly below 2. 5, the cell isn't immediately a hazard but it's being damaged.
The protective SEI layer on the anode breaks down, and at very low voltage the copper current collector can dissolve into the electrolyte. Capacity and power drop.
The real danger comes if you then charge it: that copper can redeposit as dendrites and create an internal short, which can heat or ignite later.
That's why chargers refuse to charge cells below a minimum and why protection circuits cut off at low voltage.
In a series pack it's trickier, because the pack voltage can look normal while one weak cell is over or under its limit.
So you need per-cell monitoring, a good charger with CC/CV and termination, and a low-voltage cutoff in the load."
